## How I work

### The screen comes after the questions.

I start with the problem. I study the system, speak with its users, explore directions, and test the strongest one.

- Understand the problem and the people affected by it.

- Find the system limits and connected workflows.

- Explore several approaches before choosing a direction.

- Test the design and use the findings to refine it.

- Explain the decision, support delivery, and review the build.

AI speeds up research and production. Design judgment, source checks, and final decisions stay with the team.

# Restaurant problems.
Evidence to release.

I design restaurant software with the people who use it, then stay close through testing, implementation, and release.

Best place to start Bar Tabs

The clearest end-to-end story of field research, prototypes, testing, and shipped work.

[Open Bar Tabs →](https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/)

Role evidence

## The work matches the full product cycle.

Each point below links to the case study with the strongest proof.

01 · Research

### Talk with restaurant teams

Bar Tabs includes interviews with 15 waitstaff and managers, customer sessions, competitive research, Smart Serve training, and work behind a bar.

[See the field research →](https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/#decisions)

02 · Prototype

### Make ideas testable early

Kiosk quantity controls moved through five concepts, eight refinements, paper tests, hardware trials, two voting rounds, and one shipped rule set.

[See the Kiosk test →](https://meshgi.com/kiosk/#decisions)

03 · Delivery

### Stay through implementation

POS and Backoffice work records responsive rules, component behavior, engineering handoff, staged releases, and build review.

[See shipped platform patterns →](https://meshgi.com/pos/#product)

04 · Product depth

### Learn the operating system

The work connects POS, Kiosk, Bar Tabs, and Backoffice. Each decision accounts for permissions, hardware, service states, and connected workflows.

[Compare the four products →](https://meshgi.com/product-design/#projects)

05 · AI

### Use AI inside the work

I use connected sources to synthesize research, compare concepts, check current product rules, build prototypes, and preserve decisions.

[Read the AI practice →](https://meshgi.com/ai-design-practice/)

06 · Systems

### Return patterns to the system

The shared POS keyboard, responsive guidance, Menu Management components, and navigation rules reduce repeated design and engineering decisions.

[See the component decisions →](https://meshgi.com/backoffice/#decisions)

07 · Critique

### Show unfinished work

The Quick Menu record keeps rejected directions, critique notes, and the reason version six won. The case studies explain tradeoffs, limits, and open measures.

[See the iteration record →](https://meshgi.com/backoffice/#decisions)

08 · Shipping

### Separate release from intent

Every case study labels released, partial, proposed, and unmeasured work. Kiosk and POS include dated production footprints.

[See the release evidence →](https://meshgi.com/kiosk/#result)

# Page: AI Design Practice | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "AI Design Practice | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "How senior product designer Parmis Meshgi uses AI for research synthesis, concept exploration, design systems, prototypes, code, and decision records."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/ai-design-practice/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/ai-design-practice/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> How senior product designer Parmis Meshgi uses AI for research synthesis, concept exploration, design systems, prototypes, code, and decision records.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/ai-design-practice/](https://meshgi.com/ai-design-practice/)

[← Hiring guide](https://meshgi.com/restaurant-product-design/)

AI design practice

# More context.
Less repeated work.

I use AI to read the real sources, test more directions, build working prototypes, and keep decisions available after a project ends.

Working rule AI does not invent the product.

It uses verified requirements, current screens, known components, and review from people who own the decision.

The working loop

## AI has a job at each useful step.

The designer still owns the question, evidence, choice, and final review.

- 01

### Read the sources

Connected Figma, Jira, meeting records, product documentation, and code give the work current context.

- 02

### Synthesize research

AI groups interview notes, repeated pain points, constraints, and open questions. I check the source before using a claim.

- 03

### Explore more than one answer

I ask for distinct concepts, failure states, and tradeoffs. Weak directions end before the team spends time polishing them.

- 04

### Use the real system

Instructions name current components, tokens, flows, and product rules. New patterns require a clear gap and team review.

- 05

### Build and test behavior

AI-assisted code turns selected flows into interactive prototypes. I test responsive behavior, states, keyboard use, and recovery.

- 06

### Keep the decision

Finished work becomes a searchable record with the reason, source, owner, limits, and release state.

What this changes

## AI helps the team spend time on decisions.

Research

### Faster synthesis

Interview notes, product history, and connected stories become a source-linked brief before design starts.

Concepts

### More real alternatives

The team can compare several behaviors and their edge cases before committing to a visual direction.

Prototype

### Working interaction

The Kiosk case includes a coded flow for service type, menu, options, order, payment, and recovery.

[Try the Kiosk proof →](https://meshgi.com/kiosk/#product)

System

### Current patterns

Product instructions stop each new task from restarting with guessed components or old behavior.

Code

### Closer to implementation

I use AI-assisted code to test interaction and responsive rules. Engineers still own product code review and release.

Memory

### Decisions stay searchable

The next project can reuse the reason behind a rule instead of copying a screen without its context.

Guardrails

## Speed only helps when the work stays true.

Source before claim

Important facts link back to product, research, or release evidence.

Existing component first

The system stays consistent unless the product has a verified component gap.

Human decision owner

AI can compare options. The responsible designer, product manager, or engineer approves the decision.

Release state stays visible

Shipped, partial, proposed, and unmeasured work keep separate labels.

Recorded practice

## 7 platforms studied.
47 design versions.
200 users tested.

These numbers come from my April 2026 design Town Hall. They describe the work behind one polished screen.

[Return to hiring guide →](https://meshgi.com/restaurant-product-design/)

> A self-service Kiosk UX and product design case study by senior product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/kiosk/](https://meshgi.com/kiosk/)

[← All work](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

Work 01 · Self-service

# Self-service
Kiosk

Self-service ordering must explain each choice, respond to physical input, and recover without staff help.

[Read the case study ↓](https://meshgi.com/kiosk/#value)

![Volanté self-service Kiosk displaying the start screen](https://meshgi.com/assets/kiosk-card-device.webp)

My role Product and UX design

Research, interaction design, accessibility, recovery, and release review

Product Self-service ordering

Kiosk, mobile, and web channels

Period 2022 to 2026

Work with design, product, engineering, and quality assurance

Scale 692 active self-service devices

Including Flip, across 422 live Volanté locations on September 14, 2026

Product at scale

## Kiosk and self-service now handle nearly half of Volanté's transaction volume.

692 Active self-service devices, including Flip

422 Live Volanté locations

17,470,823 Self-service transactions

49.5% Of Volanté transaction volume

Volanté platform data from January 1 to September 14, 2026.

Project value

## Help customers order without needing staff to explain the interface.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Reuse one menu structure across kiosk, mobile, and web.

- ✓

Keep ordering readable through high contrast and clear controls.

- ✓

Give customers clear recovery steps when hardware or payment fails.

Problem

### The interface stands alone.

Each state must explain the next action because staff guidance is not always available.

Risk

### Small failures can stop an order.

Unclear prompts, physical input, and hardware faults can block checkout.

Direction

### Make feedback part of the system.

Shared rules connect readable screens, tested controls, and guided recovery.

Design decisions

## Connect channel rules, accessibility, testing, and recovery.

01

### Design the menu once

Shared structure

Backoffice defines item groups and menu tiles. The same structure supports kiosk, mobile, and web ordering.

Intended impact

Teams configure one menu while each channel keeps suitable interaction rules.

02

### Make readability a system rule

Accessible ordering

The high-contrast theme replaces local menu colours through the existing theme switch.

Intended impact

Customers can read and complete the full ordering journey in high contrast.

03

### Test controls on the hardware

Real conditions

We refined eight quantity selectors, printed them, and tested them on the kiosk before choosing one.

Intended impact

The selected control reflects real distance, scale, and touch conditions.

04

### Guide hardware recovery

Clear next steps

The scale flow now covers placing food, lifting it, holding still, capture, and temporary or persistent faults.

Intended impact

Customers can recover without guessing what the kiosk expects.

Interactive product

## Use the self-service Kiosk.

Choose a service type, build an order, change its quantity, and complete checkout with public sample menu content.

Interactive Kiosk

00

Start screen

Enter the same full-screen Kiosk journey used in the product.

- Start

- Service

- Menu

- Order

- Payment

- Done

The layout, accessibility panel, option drawer, quantity controls, order table, and receipt actions follow the local Kiosk codebase.

Reset Kiosk

Result

## Released improvements and verified handoff replaced isolated screens.

Released

### High-contrast ordering

High-contrast and feedback improvements reached production.

Handoff

### Scale recovery

The guided hardware recovery flow reached engineering handoff.

Quality review

### Sixteen fixes completed

A production review found 19 related defects. Sixteen reached completion.

[Next work project Bar Tabs →](https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/)

# Page: Bar Tabs UX Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---

description: "A Bar Tabs and Table Service UX and product design case study by senior product designer Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/"

> A Bar Tabs and Table Service UX and product design case study by senior product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/](https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/)

[← All work](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

Work 02 · Service

# Bar Tabs &
Table Service

Staff need one clear place to find a tab, understand its state, and take the next action.

[Read the case study ↓](https://meshgi.com/bar-tabs/#value)

![Table Service concept showing live tables and service states](https://meshgi.com/assets/bar-tabs-floor.png)

My role Research and design lead

Workflow architecture, testing, direction, and release review

Research 15 staff interviews

Customer sessions, expert workshops, and ten competing products

Period 2024 to 2026

Work with design, product, and engineering

Status Released and evolving

Bar Tabs shipped. Table Service remains in design

Project value

## Reduce errors and keep service moving during a busy shift.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Make every open bill easy to find and understand.

- ✓

Protect restricted actions without forcing staff to lose their place.

- ✓

Carry service status from tabs into a clear table view.

Problem

### Service changes by the second.

Tabs move between staff, payment states, and service areas during the same shift.

Risk

### Slow recovery affects guests.

Unpaid tabs, unclear ownership, and restricted actions create delay and errors.

Direction

### Keep state and action together.

One overview shows each bill, its owner, its status, and the actions available.

Design decisions

## Turn service research into visible rules for every tab.

01

### Research the pressure

Field understanding

I reviewed ten products, interviewed 15 staff, earned Smart Serve, and worked behind a bar.

Intended impact

The design reflects service speed, errors, training, and low-light conditions.

02

### Build one working overview

Visible state

The Bar Tabs Visualizer combines tile and list views, search, quick view, filters, ownership, and status.

Intended impact

Staff can find a bill and understand its current state quickly.

03

### Replace drag with selection

Lower learning effort

Testing changed bill splitting from drag and drop to a select-and-assign model.

Intended impact

The split stays explicit and requires less new interaction learning.

04

### Keep approval in context

Recover safely

Restricted access originally forced a logout. Manager approval now happens inside the active workflow.

Intended impact

Staff can recover without losing the tab or their place.

05

### Extend the same model

Table service

Table Service carries bills, seats, and service status into a floor view with defined recovery states.

Intended impact

The spatial view uses the same service rules instead of creating a separate system.

Product proof

## The service model works from tab overview to floor planning.

![Table Service concept with tables in several service states](https://meshgi.com/assets/bar-tabs-floor.png)

Live service

Each table shows ownership, timing, and payment state at a glance.

![Earlier floor-plan editor concept with object tools and table controls](https://meshgi.com/assets/floor-editor.png)

Earlier exploration

This concept tested the authoring model before its placement changed.

Result

## Bar Tabs shipped, while Table Service remains a defined extension.

Released

### Bar Tabs

The first release supports single-server tabs and clear payment states.

Defined next

### Table Service

The unshipped extension includes floor, seat, permission, offline, and conflict states.

Measure next

### Service signals

Future measures include recall success, closing time, permission failures, and recovery completion.

[Work index See all product design work →](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

[Next work project Backoffice →](https://meshgi.com/backoffice/)

# Page: Backoffice UX Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

> A Backoffice Menu Management UX and product design case study by senior product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/backoffice/](https://meshgi.com/backoffice/)

[← All work](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

Work 03 · Administration

# Backoffice
Menu Management

Administrators need clear structure when one menu change can affect many records, stores, and service channels.

[Read the case study ↓](https://meshgi.com/backoffice/#value)

![Menu Management grid with sample records and selection controls](https://meshgi.com/assets/menu-grid.png)

My role Lead product designer

Workshops, interaction rules, responsive guidance, and handoff

Product Backoffice

Restaurant administration and menu configuration

Period 2025 to 2026

Work with design, product, engineering, and quality assurance

Status Partial release

Navigation and configuration work shipped in stages

Project value

## Make dense menu work predictable without hiding its connections.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Separate navigation, record scanning, and detailed editing.

- ✓

Give every table row the same selection and navigation behavior.

- ✓

Preserve one source for shared options across connected products.

Problem

### Every record has connections.

Items, categories, prices, choices, stores, and service channels affect each other.

Risk

### Small inconsistencies spread.

Mixed row behavior and repeated controls slow work and increase editing mistakes.

Direction

### Assign each area one job.

The interface separates structure, scanning, preview, and full editing.

Design decisions

## Use stable interaction rules across a dense administration product.

01

### Separate the editing layers

Clear structure

The left tree selects an area, the grid supports scanning, and the right panel previews one record.

Intended impact

People keep their place while moving from overview to detail.

02

### Give each row one behavior

Predictable navigation

One click selects and previews. The arrow or See Details opens the full page.

Intended impact

Rows stay stable and can still support inline editing.

03

### Define bulk actions first

Controlled scale

The team prioritized named bulk actions before an unrestricted edit-anything model.

Intended impact

Large changes remain clear, reviewable, and easier to deliver.

04

### Use one flexible Quick Menu

Cross-channel reuse

The selected direction uses one flexible column, insertion, reorderable tabs, multi-select, and search.

Intended impact

One structure adapts across POS, kiosk, mobile, and future sizes.

05

### Sequence responsive work

Delivery focus

The team defined Menu Management components before updating the full shared system.

Intended impact

Engineering receives useful guidance without waiting for a complete system rewrite.

Product proof

## The grid makes scanning, selection, and connected data visible.

![Menu Management grid with sample names, prices, tags, and selection states](https://meshgi.com/assets/menu-grid.png)

Record library

Selection, tags, prices, and related data stay visible in one scanning view.

Result

## A shared foundation reached delivery in stages.

Delivered

### Navigation and configuration

Navigation, category, and linked-option work reached delivery in stages.

Expanded

### Combo Sets

Combo Sets gained a list, detail view, permissions, and multi-store actions.

Measure next

### Administration signals

Future measures include bulk completion, navigation errors, and time to find an item.

[Work index See all product design work →](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

[Next work project POS →](https://meshgi.com/pos/)

# Page: Point of Sale UX Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---

last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> A responsive point-of-sale UX and product design case study by senior product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/pos/](https://meshgi.com/pos/)

[← All work](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

Work 04 · Core platform

# Point of
Sale

I built responsive rules for the screens that move a restaurant from login to payment.

[Read the case study ↓](https://meshgi.com/pos/#value)

![Volanté login interface displayed on a point-of-sale terminal while a card is scanned](https://meshgi.com/assets/pos-card-device.webp)

My role Product and UX design

Responsive rules, workflows, handoff, and release review

Product Volanté POS

Restaurant order entry and service

Period 2023 to 2026

Work with design, product, engineering, and quality assurance

Scale 1,064 active POS terminals

Plus 84 active Cloud POS devices on September 14, 2026

Product at scale

## The shared POS system reached production and now supports a large active footprint.

1,064 Active POS terminals

84 Active Cloud POS devices

17,773,950 POS transactions

50.4% Of Volanté transaction volume

Volanté Product Specialist data from January 1 to September 14, 2026. The active footprint covers 422 live locations.

Project value

## Make fast restaurant work stay clear across screens, modes, and input devices.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Scale type, spacing, popups, and controls across three terminal sizes.

- ✓

Use one keyboard and keypad across login, search, payment, and approval.

- ✓

Organize each workflow around its ticket, states, behavior, and prototype.

Problem

### One product serves many tasks.

Order entry, search, payment, approval, customer accounts, printing, and service modes share one system.

Risk

### Every exception costs time.

Different layouts and input behavior slow staff during busy service and create more training work.

Direction

### Turn patterns into a system.

Responsive guidance and shared components reduce repeated decisions across product and engineering.

Design decisions

## Build reusable rules before adjusting individual screens.

01

### Start from real terminal sizes

Responsive foundation

The 26-page responsive file covers 1366 by 768, 1366 by 1024, and 1024 by 768 terminals.

Intended impact

Each layout decision has a clear reference size and manual device check.

02

### Research search behavior

Pattern study

A 142-participant placement study guided search position, button behavior, and suggestions.

Intended impact

Staff find search where they expect it and understand how results will respond.

03

### Share one keyboard

Common input

The Bar Tabs keyboard became the shared POS input for search, cash payment, manager override, and login in GA13.

Intended impact

Staff reuse the same input pattern across devices and tasks.

04

### Design for physical inputs

Device behavior

Touch, keyboards, scanners, cards, drawers, printers, scales, and payment devices all need clear ownership and recovery.

Intended impact

Disconnected, delayed, duplicate, and retry states become part of the workflow.

Product proof

## The design system grew from guidelines into shipped platform patterns.

Responsive system

### 2,508 frames

The 26-page guidelines cover sizes, gutters, popups, keyboards, keypads, and shared behavior.

Workflow authority

### 6,474 frames

The 36-page Quick Menu file holds ticket-based work across orders, customers, transactions, discounts, gift cards, and printing.

Released entry point

### Login and home

The Bar Tabs redesign became the POS login and home across service modes in February 2026.

Result

## The shared system reached production and now supports a large active footprint.

Released

### GA13 keyboard

One responsive keyboard replaced the legacy pattern across major POS input tasks.

Responsive coverage

### Three terminal sizes

The released guidance covers 1366 by 768, 1366 by 1024, and 1024 by 768 terminals.

Research

### 142 participants

The placement study guided search position, button behavior, and suggestions.

[Work index See all product design work →](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

[Return to all work Work index →](https://meshgi.com/product-design/)

# Page: Footsteps Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Footsteps Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Footsteps is a private location journal for iPhone and iPad, designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/footsteps/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/footsteps/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Footsteps is a private location journal for iPhone and iPad, designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/footsteps/](https://meshgi.com/footsteps/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · iOS

# Footsteps

Remember where life happened without giving that history to another service.

[Open on the App Store ↗](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/footsteps/id6756509983)

![Footsteps app icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/footsteps.jpg)

![Footsteps map showing a recorded route](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/footsteps-ipad-1.jpg)

My role Product and UX design

Concept, flow, interface, and release story

Platform iPhone and iPad

Automatic location journal

Release July 21, 2026

Version 1.0.31 verified September 10

Core value Useful memory

With local-only data ownership

Project value

## Make location history useful without trading away privacy.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Record a day with little manual work.

- ✓

Turn raw location points into a readable personal story.

- ✓

Keep ownership clear through local storage and direct export.

Problem

### Memory takes effort.

Manual check-ins interrupt the day. Most people will not build a complete location journal by hand.

Risk

### Location reveals routines.

A useful record can also expose home, work, travel, and repeated habits.

Direction

### Automate with restraint.

The product should collect enough context to help, while keeping the record on the device.

Design decisions

## Connect each design choice to its intended value.

01

### Remove manual check-ins

Less input effort

Footsteps records visits and movement in the background. The user does not rebuild the day by hand.

Intended impact

More complete days with fewer repeated actions.

02

### Turn tracking into a timeline

Faster recall

Places, travel modes, duration, and maps form one chronological story.

Intended impact

Users can understand where time went without reading raw location data.

03

### Explain privacy before permission

Clearer trust

The opening flow explains local storage, no cloud sync, no analytics, and no account.

Intended impact

People see the privacy boundary before granting sensitive access.

04

### Keep the record portable

Data ownership

CSV and JSON exports let people take places, visits, and activities elsewhere.

Intended impact

The journal remains useful outside the app.

Product proof

## The released screens carry the same value story.

![Footsteps map showing a full recorded route](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/footsteps-ipad-1.jpg)

Map

A full route shows where the day happened.

![Footsteps daily journal introduction](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/footsteps-screen-1.jpg)

Journal

The product explains automatic capture through a familiar daily view.

![Footsteps privacy promise](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/footsteps-screen-2.jpg)

Privacy

Local storage and no analytics appear as product features.

Result

## A focused utility reached the App Store.

Released evidence

### Public iOS product

Footsteps launched for iPhone and iPad on July 21, 2026.

Verified boundary

### Local-only privacy

The public product states no accounts, cloud sync, analytics, tracking, or ads.

Measure next

### Value signals

Track complete days, correction rates, battery impact, exports, and repeat use. Public results are not yet available.

[Released product Open Footsteps on the App Store ↗](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/footsteps/id6756509983)

[Next side quest Seej →](https://meshgi.com/seej/)

# Page: Seej Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Seej Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Seej is a private smoking-pattern tracker for iPhone, designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/seej/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/seej/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Seej is a private smoking-pattern tracker for iPhone, designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/seej/](https://meshgi.com/seej/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · iOS

# Seej

Understand smoking patterns without turning reflection into punishment.

[Open on the App Store ↗](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/seej/id6793917651)

![Seej app icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/seej.jpg)

![Seej one-tap smoking log](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/seej-screen-1.jpg)

My role Product and UX design

Concept, flow, interface, and release story

Platform iPhone and iPad

Private habit tracker

Release August 18, 2026

Version 0.1.1 verified September 2

Core value Awareness first

With calm, neutral feedback

Project value

## Make a difficult habit easier to observe honestly.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Record a smoke before the moment passes.

- ✓

Show patterns without blame or medical claims.

- ✓

Keep every log on the user’s device.

Problem

### Small moments disappear.

A tracker loses value when recording takes longer than the habit itself.

Risk

### Judgment blocks honesty.

Harsh language can make people avoid the record they need to understand.

Direction

### Keep the loop neutral.

Use one-tap input, clear trends, and calm language to support awareness.

Design decisions

## Reduce effort while protecting honest reflection.

01

### Log in one tap

Less input effort

The main action records a smoke at once. The same screen shows today’s count, the last time, and a clear undo.

Intended impact

More complete logs with quick recovery from accidental taps.

02

### Report patterns, not scores

Neutral feedback

Daily and weekly views show counts, common times, change, and the longest gap without grading the user.

Intended impact

Help people notice patterns without adding shame.

03

### Make location optional

Choice before context

Approximate location can add place patterns to future logs. It stays optional and never blocks logging.

Intended impact

Add useful context only when the user wants it.

04

### Keep the record private

Data ownership

Seej uses no account, backend, ads, or analytics. Users can export CSV data or delete every log.

Intended impact

Make privacy visible through product behavior.

Product proof

## The released screens keep logging and reflection separate.

![Seej log screen with one large action](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/seej-screen-1.jpg)

Log

A single action records the moment and supports undo.

![Seej reports screen with daily counts](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/seej-screen-2.jpg)

Reports

Counts and gaps show change without a score.

![Seej map with location disabled](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/seej-screen-3.jpg)

Location

The map explains when new location capture is off.

Result

## A focused private tracker reached the App Store.

Released evidence

### Public iOS product

Seej launched for iPhone and iPad on August 18, 2026.

Verified boundary

### Device-only logs

The public product states no account, backend, ads, or analytics SDK.

Measure next

### Habit signals

Track repeated use, undo rates, report visits, and exports. Public results are not yet available.

[Released product Open Seej on the App Store ↗](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/seej/id6793917651)

[Next side quest Health Exporter →](https://meshgi.com/health-exporter/)

---

> Health Exporter is a user-controlled Apple Health export tool, designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/health-exporter/](https://meshgi.com/health-exporter/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · iOS

# Health
Exporter

Move the Apple Health data you choose, on your terms.

[Open on the App Store ↗](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/health-exporter/id6788438912)

![Health Exporter app icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/health-exporter.jpg)

![Health Exporter data selection and export screen](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/health-screen-1.jpg)

My role Product and UX design

Information flow, interface, and release story

Platform iPhone and iPad

Apple Health export utility

Release August 4, 2026

Version 1.0

Core value Controlled transfer

With explicit data choices

Project value

## Give people a clear route out of a closed health-data system.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Let users choose data before the app requests access.

- ✓

Support a local file and a personal server destination.

- ✓

Keep sensitive transfer choices visible and reversible.

Problem

### Health data stays trapped.

Useful records become hard to reuse when export controls are broad or unclear.

Risk

### Access can exceed need.

A health utility can request more data or storage than the task requires.

Direction

### Show every transfer step.

Place selection, permission, destination, and file review in a clear order.

Design decisions

## Make sensitive data movement understandable.

01

### Select data before access

Purpose first

Users choose the Health data types they need before the related read permission appears.

Intended impact

Connect each permission request to a visible purpose.

02

### Offer two clear destinations

Flexible ownership

The product creates a ZIP file or sends JSON batches to the user’s own HTTPS webhook.

Intended impact

Support a simple file flow and a repeatable personal sync flow.

03

### Make exports inspectable

Transparent output

A documented JSON schema, manifest, and sample batches make the output easier to understand.

Intended impact

Reduce uncertainty before the data enters another system.

04

### Avoid a bundled service

Privacy boundary

The app has no account, analytics, ads, tracking, or bundled backend. Users can review and delete stored ZIP files.

Intended impact

Keep control with the person who owns the data.

Product proof

## The interface shows what moves and where it goes.

![Health Exporter main export screen](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/health-screen-1.jpg)

Export

The range, selected data, access, and file action share one screen.

![Health Exporter personal webhook settings](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/health-screen-2.jpg)

Destination

A personal webhook stays separate from local file export.

![Health Exporter data type selection](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/health-screen-3.jpg)

Data types

Search and selection happen before Health access.

Result

## A direct health-data utility reached the App Store.

Released evidence

### Public iOS product

Health Exporter launched for iPhone and iPad on August 4, 2026.

Verified boundary

### No bundled account

The public product states no accounts, analytics, ads, tracking, or bundled backend.

Measure next

### Transfer signals

Track completed exports, retry recovery, deleted files, and webhook errors. Public results are not yet available.

[Released product Open Health Exporter on the App Store ↗](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/health-exporter/id6788438912)

[Next side quest Family Tree →](https://meshgi.com/family-tree/)

---

> Family Tree is a private bilingual family map designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/family-tree/](https://meshgi.com/family-tree/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · Web

# Family
Tree

Help relatives understand a large family while protecting private profiles.

[Open the website ↗](https://familytree.meshgi.com)

![Family Tree product showing the fitted full family map](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/family-tree-preview.svg)

Live product preview Full family map

My role Product and UX design

Map flow, search behavior, privacy, and mobile use

Platform Responsive web

English and Persian family map

Milestone July 24, 2026

Full fitted tree restored as the landing view

Core value Family context

With a server-side privacy boundary

Project value

## Make a complex family understandable from the first view.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Show the complete fitted family map at entry.

- ✓

Support natural English and Persian family searches.

- ✓

Remove private profiles before data reaches the browser.

Problem

### Family structures grow dense.

A branch-only start can hide how people connect across generations.

Risk

### Profiles carry private facts.

Hiding a card in the interface cannot protect data that the browser already received.

Direction

### Fit first, then explore.

Open with the whole family and let search guide relatives to trusted links.

Design decisions

## Balance broad context with careful access.

01

### Open on the complete tree

Context first

Phones, tablets, and desktop begin with the fitted whole-family view. Branch links still support focused exploration.

Intended impact

Help relatives understand the full structure before they zoom into one branch.

02

### Keep each family identity visible

Clear orientation

The Meshgi and Ashtari addresses share one system. Each address keeps its family label visible on small and large screens.

Intended impact

Confirm which family surface a relative opened before they explore or share it.

03

### Protect profiles on the server

Real privacy

The public data response removes private profiles, related aliases, and copied identity text before the browser receives the tree.

Intended impact

Make privacy part of the data boundary instead of a visual switch.

04

### Accept natural family questions

Flexible search

Search supports name order, English and Persian family terms, and reviewed parent, spouse, sibling, child, and ancestor links.

Intended impact

Let relatives ask in familiar words without changing recorded family facts.

Product proof

## Verified behavior carries the privacy and orientation work.

Whole map

### 115 public profiles

Production checks verify one complete public projection without technical or private records.

Two identities

### One shared tree

Meshgi and Ashtari addresses present the same trusted data with the correct family label.

Natural search

### Reviewed links

Family questions use structured relationships and stay empty when required facts are not verified.

Result

## A living family map works across two family identities.

Live evidence

### Responsive web product

The complete tree opens on phone, tablet, and desktop for both family addresses.

Verified boundary

### Private data stays out

Public health and tree responses match the server-side public profile set.

Measure next

### Family usefulness

Track successful searches, correction requests, shared branches, and empty queries. Public usage results are not available.

[Live product Open Family Tree ↗](https://familytree.meshgi.com)

# Page: Fitness Website Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Fitness Website Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Fitness Website is a private shared health dashboard designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/fitness/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/fitness/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Fitness Website is a private shared health dashboard designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/fitness/](https://meshgi.com/fitness/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · Web

# Fitness

Keep two personal health records clear inside one shared daily view.

[Open the website ↗](https://fitness.meshgi.com)

![Fitness progress rings icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/fitness.svg)

My role Product and UX design

Information model, controls, states, and privacy

Platform Private responsive web

Shared health and food record

Milestone August 20, 2026

One date pattern across the product

Core value Shared clarity

With distinct personal records

Project value

## Make daily health context useful without mixing two people’s records.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Keep Day, Food, and Progress easy to reach.

- ✓

Show one person’s food record at a time.

- ✓

Use the same date controls in every daily view.

Problem

### Daily context is scattered.

Movement, meals, totals, and progress lose meaning when each uses a different route.

Risk

### Shared can become mixed.

Two people can use one dashboard only when each record stays clear.

Direction

### Reduce the surface.

Keep three main views, one date pattern, and direct person selection.

Design decisions

## Use a small structure for repeated daily work.

01

### Keep three main views

Less navigation

The public dashboard keeps Day, Food, and Progress as its main routes.

Intended impact

Place the most common daily questions one step away.

02

### Separate each person’s food record

Clear ownership

Person tabs show only the selected person’s totals and meals.

Intended impact

Prevent a shared meal record from becoming a mixed personal record.

03

### Reuse one date pattern

Predictable control

Day, Food, and Progress place previous, next, calendar, and Today controls in the same position.

Intended impact

Let users change dates without relearning each section.

04

### Keep data movement protected

Private operations

The visible dashboard stays read-only. Protected agent and back-office routes handle imports and writes.

Intended impact

Keep everyday review simple while limiting sensitive actions.

Product proof

## The product structure supports daily review and safe correction.

Day

### One daily overview

The current date leads movement, status, and any urgent review cue.

Food

### One person at a time

Totals, meals, and the selected person stay together during date changes.

Progress

### Shared date controls

The same arrows, calendar, and Today action support comparison over time.

Result

## A private dashboard supports repeated health decisions.

Live evidence

### Three focused views

The production product uses the approved Day, Food, and Progress structure.

Verified boundary

### Protected writes

The visible dashboard stays read-only while private routes manage data changes.

Measure next

### Daily usefulness

Track date changes, review cues, corrections, and repeat visits. Public usage results are not available.

[Private product Open Fitness Website ↗](https://fitness.meshgi.com)

[Next side quest Orange Institute →](https://meshgi.com/orange-institute/)

# Page: Orange Institute UX Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Orange Institute UX Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Orange Institute is a bilingual language-school website and placement flow designed by Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/orange-institute/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/orange-institute/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Orange Institute is a bilingual language-school website and placement flow designed by Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/orange-institute/](https://meshgi.com/orange-institute/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · Web

# Orange

Help each learner find a suitable class before asking them to commit.

[Open the website ↗](https://orangeinstitute.ir)

![Orange Institute icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/orange.png)

![Children learning at Orange Institute](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/orange-hero.jpg)

My role Product and UX design

Site structure, bilingual flow, and placement logic

Platform Responsive web

Farsi and English school website

Release August 7, 2026

Rebuilt website and placement flow

Core value Better class fit

With staff confirmation

Project value

## Turn a broad school website into a guided class decision.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Serve local learners in Farsi first, with complete English routes.

- ✓

Route children and adults through suitable placement questions.

- ✓

Keep test results provisional until staff review.

Problem

### Class choice starts vague.

Language, age, level, goal, and schedule all affect the right next step.

Risk

### A test can overpromise.

A written result cannot confirm speaking, listening, or the final class by itself.

Direction

### Guide, then confirm.

Use a short placement flow and make human review part of the answer.

Design decisions

## Match the flow to a real school conversation.

01

### Make Farsi the default

Local access

The main routes open in Farsi. English uses complete routes under the English section.

Intended impact

Meet the main local audience without removing bilingual access.

02

### Ask age before test questions

Correct route

The flow collects exact age before the test. Children aged three to five receive an oral-program result without a written test.

Intended impact

Avoid giving young learners questions that do not fit the school program.

03

### Branch after each answer

Shorter path

Each response can confirm, rescue, move to the next level, or reach a course result.

Intended impact

Ask only the next useful question.

04

### Keep staff in the result

Responsible placement

The closest course appears as a provisional result. Staff confirm speaking, listening, and the final class.

Intended impact

Use the test to guide a decision without presenting it as final.

Product proof

## The live experience connects the school story to one next action.

Home

### Find a class

The main page names the languages, audience, location, and direct class-finder action.

Placement

### Age-led route

The test uses age and current answers to choose the next question or course result.

Access

### Four tested widths

Public pages passed Farsi and English checks at 320, 390, 960, and 1280 pixels.

Result

## A bilingual school website now leads with class fit.

Live evidence

### Public bilingual product

The website serves Farsi and English information, class routes, and placement.

Verified boundary

### Provisional result

The test recommends the closest course while staff keep the final placement decision.

Measure next

### Placement value

Track flow completion, staff corrections, class inquiries, and route exits. Public results are not available.

# Page: Hitchi Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Hitchi Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Hitchi is a Persian music timeline card game and scanner designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/hitchi/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/hitchi/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Hitchi is a Persian music timeline card game and scanner designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/hitchi/](https://meshgi.com/hitchi/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · Game and web

# Hitchi

Bring Persian music history to the table without revealing the answer too soon.

[Open the preview ↗](https://hitchi.rooy.dad)

![Hitchi app icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/hitchi.png)

![Hitchi website showing the scanner and game cards](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/hitchi-home.jpg)

My role Product and UX design

Game loop, card system, scanner, and website

Platform Physical game and PWA

Bilingual Persian music product

Milestone June 13, 2026

Current preserved product record began

Core value Spoiler-safe play

Scan, listen, place, then reveal

Project value

## Turn music memory into a shared timeline game.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Keep song details hidden until the player commits to a guess.

- ✓

Connect physical cards to a fast mobile scan loop.

- ✓

Support Persian and English players in the same room.

Problem

### Playback can spoil the game.

Music services can reveal the song, artist, artwork, or year before the guess.

Risk

### Digital can replace the table.

A heavy app can pull attention away from cards, debate, and shared memory.

Direction

### Use the phone as a bridge.

Let the card start playback, protect the answer, and return attention to the group.

Design decisions

## Protect the surprise across cards, sound, and screen.

01

### Hide answer metadata

Spoiler control

The pre-reveal scan response hides title, artist, year, artwork, and other answer clues.

Intended impact

Preserve the guess even when playback begins on a phone.

02

### Keep the turn loop physical

Table-first play

The player scans, listens, places the card in time, and then reveals the answer.

Intended impact

Use the screen for support while the shared timeline stays central.

03

### Design for two reading directions

Bilingual play

The experience supports Persian and English. The Persian timeline places older music on the right and newer music on the left.

Intended impact

Keep the game natural for mixed-language groups.

04

### Separate preview from release

Honest status

The working scanner and website remain a preview while catalog approval, rights, and print checks stay open.

Intended impact

Show the product without presenting candidate material as release-ready.

Product proof

## The current preview carries one clear turn from scan to reveal.

![Hitchi website with cards and scanner](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/hitchi-home.jpg)

Product story

The site explains the card game before it asks people to launch the scanner.

![Hitchi scanner start screen in Persian](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/hitchi-app.jpg)

Scan

The mobile tool begins with the scan action and player controls.

![Hitchi hidden song screen before reveal](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/hitchi-scan.jpg)

Guess

The answer stays hidden while players place the song in time.

Result

## A complete product direction now connects the card and scanner.

Working evidence

### Playable preview

The current package includes the game rules, card system, scanner flow, and bilingual website.

Verified boundary

### Release gates stay open

Catalog, print, privacy, and music-rights checks still block a final public release.

Measure next

### Table play

Test scan success, time to first song, spoiler failures, rule questions, and replay. Public results are not available.

[Technical preview Open Hitchi ↗](https://hitchi.rooy.dad)

[Next side quest Rooy.dad →](https://meshgi.com/rooydad/)

# Page: Rooy.dad Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Rooy.dad Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Rooy.dad is a bilingual guide to Persian community events in Toronto, designed by Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/rooydad/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/rooydad/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Rooy.dad is a bilingual guide to Persian community events in Toronto, designed by Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/rooydad/](https://meshgi.com/rooydad/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · Web

# Rooy.dad

Help Toronto’s Persian community find what is happening next.

[Open the website ↗](https://rooy.dad/en)

![Rooy.dad icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/rooydad.ico)

My role Product and UX design

Directory structure, bilingual flow, and submission model

Platform Responsive web

English and Persian event guide

Milestone August 5, 2026

Current shared product record began

Core value Community discovery

With human-reviewed listings

Project value

## Make local Persian events easy to find and safe to publish.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Offer the same event guide in English and Persian.

- ✓

Make search, calendar, and past events easy to reach.

- ✓

Review community submissions before publication.

Problem

### Events live in fragments.

Community listings often spread across social posts, messages, and separate calendars.

Risk

### Open listings lose trust.

Unreviewed submissions can publish incomplete, duplicate, or unsuitable event details.

Direction

### Curate a direct guide.

Lead with event discovery and keep human review in the submission path.

Design decisions

## Support discovery even when the event list changes.

01

### Lead with search

Direct discovery

The page asks what is on and places event search before deeper browsing.

Intended impact

Help visitors act on a date, name, or interest without scanning every listing.

02

### Keep both languages complete

Shared access

English and Persian routes share events, calendar access, empty states, and submission actions.

Intended impact

Serve a bilingual community without making one language secondary.

03

### Design the gap between event batches

Useful empty state

When no upcoming batch is live, the page explains the state and offers past events instead of a blank list.

Intended impact

Keep the guide useful between publishing cycles.

04

### Review every submission

Curated quality

Hosts can submit an event for free. A person reviews it before it goes live.

Intended impact

Grow the guide while protecting listing quality.

Product proof

## The live page handles discovery, gaps, and contribution.

Search

### What’s on

The page opens with event search and a route to the calendar view.

Empty state

### Between batches

The current page explains that more events will arrive and links to the past archive.

Contribution

### Submit for review

Hosts can propose an event and see the human-review rule before submission.

Result

## A bilingual community guide now has a clear publishing loop.

Live evidence

### Public event product

Rooy.dad serves event discovery, calendar access, archives, and submissions in two languages.

Verified boundary

### Human review

The live product states that a person reviews submitted events before publication.

Measure next

### Discovery signals

Track searches, event opens, archive use, submissions, and review time. Public results are not available.

[Live product Open Rooy.dad ↗](https://rooy.dad/en)

[Next side quest Chaashni →](https://meshgi.com/chaashni/)

# Page: Chaashni Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi

---
title: "Chaashni Product Design Case Study | Parmis Meshgi"
description: "Chaashni is a Persian recipe finder designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi."
canonical_url: "https://meshgi.com/chaashni/"
html_url: "https://meshgi.com/chaashni/"
author: "Parmis Meshgi"
location: "Toronto, Canada"
language: "en-CA"
last_updated: "2026-09-29"
---

> Chaashni is a Persian recipe finder designed by product designer Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/chaashni/](https://meshgi.com/chaashni/)

[← Side projects](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

Independent product · Web

# Chaashni

Start with the cooking decision, then help people reach a recipe they can use.

[Open the website ↗](https://chashni.rooy.dad)

![Chaashni icon](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/chaashni.png)

![Persian khoresh dish from Chaashni](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/chaashni-dish-1.jpg)

My role Product and UX design

Discovery flow, recipe structure, filters, and states

Platform Responsive web

Persian recipe finder

Milestone May 16, 2026

Current service bootstrap completed

Core value Practical choice

Before long recipe reading

Project value

## Help people answer “What can I cook?” before they read the recipe.

### What the design needed to achieve

- ✓

Show time, effort, cost, method, and servings early.

- ✓

Let practical filters narrow the recipe list.

- ✓

Help users recover when a search returns nothing.

Problem

### Recipes answer too late.

A long story cannot help when the first question is time, effort, ingredient, or method.

Risk

### More filters can add work.

A large filter system becomes another task when it does not match cooking decisions.

Direction

### Decide before reading.

Put practical facts first and keep recovery close to every empty result.

Design decisions

## Organize the product around the moment before cooking.

01

### Put recipe facts first

Fast scanning

Recipe pages show time, effort, cost, method, and servings before ingredients and steps.

Intended impact

Help users reject or choose a recipe before deep reading.

02

### Use filters as cooking questions

Practical choice

Course, intent, ingredients, timing, effort, method, and region help users express the meal they can make.

Intended impact

Turn browsing into a smaller, more useful set of choices.

03

### Recover from no results

Useful empty state

The recipe list suggests the smallest useful change, such as removing one filter or the search term.

Intended impact

Keep the cooking task moving instead of ending at a blank page.

04

### Design mobile-first for cooking

Kitchen use

The interface uses strong scanning, large tap targets, and reduced-motion support for phones and tablets.

Intended impact

Keep the recipe usable while hands and attention are busy.

Product proof

## Clear food images support a structured cooking flow.

![Persian khoresh recipe image](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/chaashni-dish-1.jpg)

Choice

A clear finished dish helps the user confirm the recipe direction.

![Persian tahchin recipe image](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/chaashni-dish-2.jpg)

Recipe

Consistent bowl images make different dishes easier to compare.

![Illustrated steps for ash reshteh](https://meshgi.com/assets/playground/chaashni-steps.jpg)

Method

Step images support the written cooking sequence.

Result

## A live Persian recipe finder supports the full choice-to-cooking path.

Live evidence

### Public recipe product

Chaashni offers home discovery, recipe filters, suggestions, recipe details, and request recovery.

Verified boundary

### Practical metadata

The product keeps cooking facts and useful recovery inside the main browsing flow.

Measure next

### Cooking signals

Track recipe opens, filter use, empty-state recovery, saved URLs, and related-recipe visits. Public results are not available.

[Live product Open Chaashni ↗](https://chashni.rooy.dad)

[Return to the index All side projects →](https://meshgi.com/playground/)

> A teaching platform and education product designed by Parmis Meshgi.

Canonical page: [https://meshgi.com/teaching/](https://meshgi.com/teaching/)

Personal practice · Teaching

# Orange Teaching Platform

I learned to design
by watching how children learn.

[Watch the story ↓](https://meshgi.com/teaching/#teaching-film-heading)

Orange Teaching Platform

Practice Teaching children

English, phonics, and Montessori methods

What I learned Watch before solving

Different learners need different paths

Story format 90-second film

A paper-cut timeline from teaching to design

Connected project Orange Institute

A bilingual website and placement flow

## Growing up with Orange

A 90-second paper-cut film about my mother’s English school, the years I taught there, and how teaching led me to design.

Parmis & Orange

A 90-second paper-cut film

Play Tap for sound

Turn the pages

### Parmis & Orange

How a child in her mother's classroom became a teacher, then a designer.

Page 1

#### A notebook full of words

When Parmis was seven, her first English teacher was her mother. Every new word went into a little notebook.

Page 2

#### A school called Orange

When Parmis was twelve, her mother opened a school and named it Orange. Its rooms filled with stories, songs, and curious questions.

Page 3

#### The teacher learns too

At university, Parmis returned to Orange as a teacher. She saw that each child needed a different way into the lesson.

Page 4

#### Small hands, big clues

Phonics made letters speak. Montessori let children lead with their hands. Parmis learned to watch before she solved.

Page 5

#### The classroom moved

Then every desk moved onto a screen. The children tried hard, but the screen did not know how young learners played, moved, or asked for help.

Page 6

#### A new question

Parmis wondered, "What if the screen could learn from its users too?" That question led her to UX design.

Page 7

#### A new chapter

She moved to Canada, studied UX, and designed a learning platform around what children and teachers had shown her.

Page 8

#### Back to Orange

Years later, Parmis returned with design, code, and AI. The school helped her grow. Now she helps it grow too.

01

## The learning problem

Your project context will define the learners, need, and constraints.

02

## The platform system

Your project context will define the experience, tools, and design decisions.

03

## Teaching in practice

Your project context will define the lessons, feedback, and outcomes.

Continue with the product

I returned to my family’s school to design its bilingual website and class-placement flow.
